routes.label: Unfold two faces and prove minimality

question:
An insect lives on the surface of a regular tetrahedron with edges of length \(1.\) It wishes to travel on the surface of the tetrahedron from the midpoint of one edge to the midpoint of the opposite edge. What is the length of the shortest such trip? (Note: Two edges of a tetrahedron are opposite if they have no common endpoint.)

[Figure 1](figures/2001_AMC_12_Q15_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
Label the tetrahedron's vertices \(A,B,C,D\), with starting point \(P\) the midpoint of \(AB\) and destination \(Q\) the midpoint of \(CD\). Unfold faces \(ABC\) and \(ACD\) along their common edge \(AC\). Unfolding preserves lengths on each face and makes it possible to compare paths with a straight segment.

Write \(D'\) and \(Q'\) for the unfolded positions of \(D\) and \(Q\). The two equilateral triangles form a rhombus \(ABCD'\) of side length \(1\). Let \(N\) be the midpoint of \(AC\). In triangle \(ABC\), the midpoint theorem gives
\[
PN=\frac{BC}{2}=\frac12,
\qquad PN\parallel BC.
\]
In triangle \(ACD'\), it gives
\[
NQ'=\frac{AD'}2=\frac12,
\qquad NQ'\parallel AD'.
\]
Opposite sides of the rhombus are parallel, so \(P,N,Q'\) lie on one straight line. Since the two triangles lie on opposite sides of \(AC\), \(N\) lies between \(P\) and \(Q'\). Hence
\[
PQ'=PN+NQ'=1.
\]
Folding this segment back gives an allowed surface trip of length \(1\).

To prove that no other route is shorter, consider any surface trip from \(P\) to \(Q\). It must pass from one of the two faces containing \(AB\) to one of the two faces containing \(CD\). Therefore it meets at least one of \(AC,AD,BC,BD\), possibly at a vertex. Call such a point \(X\). By interchanging the names within the pairs \(A,B\) and \(C,D\), we may call that edge \(AC\).

The portion before \(X\) has length at least the straight distance \(PX\), and the portion after it has length at least \(XQ\). These segments lie in faces \(ABC\) and \(ACD\). Unfold those faces as above. The triangle inequality in the plane gives
\[
\text{trip length}\ge PX+XQ'
\ge PQ'=1.
\]
This also covers trips through vertices or across additional faces. A length of \(1\) is attainable and no smaller length is possible, so the answer is \(\boxed{1}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
